title: Lessons from Trillion Token Deployments at Fortune 500s — Alessandro Cappelli, Adaptive ML

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that RL (RLHF, PPO, GSPO, reward models) is the systematic post-training method for continuous model improvement from MVP to production. Examples are drawn from Fortune 500 enterprise operations (AT&T, Manulife, CCS) with customer support use cases like transcript summarization and containment rate. The talk spans post-training adaptation, production serving, and continuous improvement loops driven by production feedback. Assumes familiarity with ML concepts like SFT, RL, and model serving but explains RL methodology at a conceptual rather than deeply technical level. The content is a single-speaker conference talk delivered on the AI Engineer channel. All classification claims are directly stated in the transcript with specific evidence anchors.

summary: Alessandro Cappelli presents the thesis that the GenAI production gap is a feedback integration problem, not a prompt engineering or deployment problem. He introduces the 'myth of the last mile'—the false belief that reaching an MVP is the hard part and production is a short final step. In reality, getting from MVP to production and beyond is the real marathon, requiring accelerated model lifecycle iteration that systematically integrates client feedback, business metrics, and environmental rewards. Only RL unlocks this in a mathematical, monitorable way. Proprietary models limit you to system prompt tweaks; instruction fine-tuning requires expensive dataset recreation cycles. RL delivers disproportionately better performance than SFT or prompting, enabling smaller models that are cheaper to serve at scale, faster for latency-constrained use cases, and owned entirely by the enterprise. He cites AT&T spending millions on transcript summarization and notes speech-to-speech systems need ~1/3 second latency, impossible with large models. Agents compound all these challenges—more tokens, less error tolerance, direct database access—but RL was originally designed to train agents in environments. Enterprises can either plug into existing agent workflows or mock tools and users. Synthetic data becomes a byproduct of environment training via rejection sampling from reward-scored trajectories. The human in the loop shifts from expensive annotation campaigns to defining rubrics and scenarios for LLM judges, reducing effort from weeks to hours. RL is hard—PPO requires orchestrating four LLMs simultaneously—but Adaptive ML's Adaptive Engine platform handles this complexity through pre-built recipes for algorithms like GSPO, supporting evaluation, training, and serving on top of open-source models. In Q&A, Cappelli explains that small-scale human feedback (10-20 samples) improves LLM judges, while at production scale, thousands of feedback signals train reward models to scale that human feedback. Implicit vs explicit feedback handling depends on the specific use case.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and RL Thesis
sections.summary: Cappelli introduces himself and Adaptive ML's RL Ops platform serving enterprises like AT&T, Manulife, and CCS. He argues RL is not just another post-training algorithm but one that brings models to production. The gap between open-source and frontier proprietary models is RL, discovered while training Falcon.

sections.title: The Myth of the Last Mile
sections.summary: 95% of GenAI pilots fail because the 'last mile' myth is false—getting to MVP is the first mile, not the hard part. Proprietary models only allow prompt tweaks; instruction fine-tuning requires expensive dataset recreation. Neither integrates defects or feedback systematically. Only RL enables continuous retraining driven by client feedback, business metrics, and environmental rewards.

sections.title: RL Unlocks Smaller, Cheaper, Faster, Owned Models
sections.summary: RL delivers outsized performance vs SFT, enabling same performance with smaller models. This unlocks cheaper serving at scale (AT&T spends millions on transcript summarization), faster latency for production constraints (1/3 second for speech-to-speech requires ~10B models), and full data and solution ownership without dependency on model updates.

sections.title: Agents Raise the Stakes
sections.summary: Agents require more tokens, have less error tolerance, and access live databases, compounding tokenomics challenges. RL was originally designed to train agents in environments, making it a natural fit. Enterprises can plug into existing agent workflows (Manulife) or mock tools and users. Rewards come from business KPIs or LLM-as-judge for tone and guideline adherence.

sections.title: Synthetic Data as RL Byproduct
sections.summary: Agent training data doesn't exist in the wild. RL with an environment and reward naturally generates good trajectories via rejection sampling, creating a synthetic dataset pipeline as a byproduct. Real conversation data (e.g., panicked callers to medical supply companies) can train realistic mock users.

sections.title: Human in the Loop and Reward Design
sections.summary: RLHF's human-in-the-loop reputation masks expensive, ineffective annotation campaigns. The human role shifts to defining rubrics and scenarios for LLM judges, taking minutes to hours rather than weeks, without iterative repetition. Systematic rewards include code execution success or KPIs like CCS's containment rate. Open-ended quality dimensions (tone, business requirements) are handled by LLM-as-judge with human-defined rubrics.

sections.title: Adaptive Engine and RL Complexity
sections.summary: Adaptive ML built the Adaptive Engine, a holistic RL Ops platform to observe, train, and serve LLMs. It supports building on top of open-source models like Gemma, Mistral, and Qwen. The catch with RL is that it is hard—PPO requires orchestrating four LLMs simultaneously. Adaptive Engine handles this complexity via pre-built recipes for algorithms like GSPO, so users define rubrics while the platform manages RL training complexity.

sections.title: Q&A: Human Feedback Integration
sections.summary: An audience member asks about incorporating human feedback from production (citing Cursor's approach of using top-completion acceptance signals). Cappelli describes two scenarios: small-scale feedback (10-20 samples) is used to improve LLM judges, while at production scale (thousands of feedback signals), the data trains reward models to scale human feedback. Initially a prompted large model (~235B) serves as judge; at production scale, trained reward models replace it. Implicit feedback handling depends on the specific use case.
